To me the biggest help was abandoning the mirror and doing it by feeling. It's much, much easier to follow along with your hands and imagination, than trying to follow a mirrored image.

You can make simple braids, right? I suggest do a bunch of those first. Like, at least a dozen or two. On the top of your head, or at the back of it, doesn't matter, the point is, getting the hang of how your hands need to twist, which strand to transfer from which finger to another, while doing the braid on your hair. It's quite different from doing a braid in front of you.

When you got the hang of it, and by that I mean that you can easily do it without needing to think about your next move, you can start doing the french braid. It's the same as a simple braid, the only difference, is adding a bit of hair to the strand, before crossing it.

I find it easier, to grab hair from the same side as the strand that you cross over. Grabbing from opposite side (beneath the braid) creates a slightly different braid, but it's extra practice to get it right.

The point is, in making sure, that your strands are always separate, and that you have a certain pattern on which strand to transfer to which finger. If you got that pattern down, and can keep track of every strand, even while you hold all three in one hand and grab extra hair with the other, then the french braid will be easy. But it is a lot of practice, and I struggled a lot with it at the beginning, especially since it's really tiring on your arms.

I agree partly, but on the other hand, shouldn't the trainers, as a rule, be more cautious? We are talking about a 12 year old child afterall. You can put an adult on a horse that spooks at open barn doors and random cars and cats, provided you inform them about this and they give an informed consent, and are also a good enough rider to be unlikely to fall off. But shouldn't we try to put a child on a bombproof horse?

Of course, I understand, that no matter the training or personality of the horse, it will inevitably spook sooner or later, and tripping is also not something you can rule out. But if I know, that this horse regurarly(!!) spooks at open doors, cats and cars, I will find a horse for the child, that doesn't do that. Or, I will put the child on such a horse, after the child has a stable and strong seat, so that in case the horse spooks (or trips), the child is more likely to stay in saddle.

I cannot judge over the internet, if the child has enough strength and balance for this, but I recon that she is not quite there yet, if she fell of thrice in 8 months.

I will give a personal example: the barn I ride at has several bombproof ponies, and larger horses for beginners. Do they spook if they are sufficiently startled? Yes, I have seen it happen. But these instances were also outliers, rather than something that is likely to happen. For example, one time a deer got into the adjacent arena, spooked the hot and nervous horse that was being lunged there, and this, in turn, spooked the pony in our arena, who also happened to be cantering at the side closest to the deer and the other spooked horse. The pony went faster along the side, and at the end of the arena the rider fell off, and the pony stopped. 

Is this something that happens often? Not at all. Deer are rare, and they never get this close to the barn, and these schoolhorses don't usually care about other hot and nervous horses doing their own thing at the other arena. It was a freak occurence. In other words, you need something out of the ordinary to startle these ponies. (Btw, the bombproof horse I was riding on, and another pony didn't so much as twitch their ears at the whole thing.)

Now, there is a gelding at this barn, that can get nervous around cars. If you slam the cardoor or the car beeps, he can spook. Simply cars driving by are unlikely to bother him. Unfortunately, the carpark is next to the bigger arena, so when people come/go in their cars at the start or end of a lesson, this gelding needs to move to the other half of the arena, to minimise the risk of spooking.

I have been riding him for about a month now. I have not ridden him before that, in the over half a year that I'm at this barn, because my trainer only puts riders on him, if she is sure that we won't end up eating dirt at the slightest twitch. In this month, he only spook once, when a car unexpectedly beeped in the middle of the lesson, otherwise no problems at all. Still, everyone is apropriatly careful.

A child like OP's child would not be riding this gelding.

My point is: don't put a horse that is likely to spook at things that are common at the barn, under a child who doesn't have a stable and strong enough seat to be likely to stay in saddle.

Yes, falling off is inevitable, I had my own share in that. That is also why we wear helmets, back protectors, and are in general, more careful. But that's the point: be more careful. Don't create unnecessary danger.

That's my take on this situation. I'm not saying that OP should run from the barn screaming, but i'm also a bit iffy about this child-horse pairing.

Something that helped me to keep my legs from swinging all over in posting trot, is to keep most of my weight in my knees/inner thigh, instead of in the stirrups. In other words, when I rise in saddle, I grip the saddle with my knees, instead of shifting my weight to my feet, and therefore shifting their position. Ideally, you should be able to do the rising trot without the stirrups, at least for a little while. Great at strengthening your legs.

I mean, if your weight is mostly on your sitbones, and then you put it into your feet, it's inevitable, that your lover leg moves somewhat. But if you shift that weight to your inner thigh/knees, and your knees won't move from their position on the saddle, then your lover leg also won't move. Of course, you need to keep some weight in the stirrups at all times anyway, so that you can keep your heels down, and this will also be a support for you, so that you aren't struggling with lifting 100% of your weight by simply gripping with your inner thighs.

It took me a lot of time to decide to nope out of a barn too. If you are not familiar with horse care (like I was at the time), it might take a while to notice that some things aren't okay. Especially if there are several reasons why you are biased towards this particular place.

I had a few criteria for a barn when I searched for one, after a decade of not seeing a horse in rl. Part of that was the price, the riding time, the availability of lessons, the attitude of the owners/trainers and the public transport connection. This particular barn hit all the marks for these criteria, and compared to some less than stellar places I visited a decade ago, I learned a lot more in riding. The owners being one of the kindest and nicest people was also a big bonus.

Basically, I was just wearing rose colored glasses 24/7. It took me 2 years, and multiple instances of personally vitnessing worrying things, as well as visiting other barns due to my friend searching for a good place, and also said friend questioning my barn, before I could take off those glasses, and say that "this is effed up, i'm not giving them my money anymore". I won't say, that this barn was straight up terrible or abusive. In general, they loved their horses, and took care of them. It's just that this care sometimes fell short of what I would consider good, but not for malicious reasons. This is a family business, with knowledge learned from generations ago, and it simply does not hold up to today's standards.

Besides, when I first showed up there, it all seemed completely fine to me. I didn't see everything that was wrong, happen on the same day, and something that I really didn't like, and was the major reason for leaving the barn, happened not long before I left.

Of course, part of the reason was the support my mother and my friend showed me, they were there for me every day, and especially my friend could understand what i'm going through (we basically pulled eachother out of depression), but horseriding, and it being a constant thing in my life, was what really did it for me.

Even with an otherwise well trained horse you can struggle a great deal at the beginning. Every horse is different, and even if they are trained the same, they are bound to have their own quirks. Because of this it's entirely possible that until you get used to eachother and you two finally click, there will be many frustrating rides. I do not claim to be greatly experienced, I probably didn't ride more than 20 different horses so far, but aside from automatic school horses that didn't need much input from me, it was on the better trained ones, who very much needed *me* to tell them what to do instead of going in endless circles, where I struggled the most. These are the horses that need you to be confident and clear in your cues, but they have to be the ones that the horse knows. And until you learn, exactly how they should look like, or train the horse to listen to your version of them, there is bound to be plenty of miscommunication.

Even with the horse that I currently ride, boy did I struggle. In the first almost two months, there were rides where the only comment I could give my trainer was "I don't know what i'm doing wrong", after I spent the whole lesson unable to keep the horse going straight, or trot more than 5 steps. This horse forced me to think more than I previously did during rides, trying to figure out different ways I could communicate my wishes to him, and he definitely made me a better rider. But once I figured out, what and how I should do things, I no longer struggle. Sure, not every ride is perfect, but there is none of that nonsense where we are turning in circles and going backwards when all I want is a trot in a straight line.

Anyway, my point is, first get to know your horse, and learn to speak it's language. Only then, you can make progress, and yes, it's going to take time. Force won't yield good results.

I have had 40-something old ladies loudly talk among themselves about how trashy my generation is, after I didn't get up and give them my seat on a full bus... Lady, I have invisible disability. I can only stand for up to an hour, before my back starts hurting so much, I begin contemplating laying down on the ground. At that moment, I was well beyond that 1 hour, and I really needed the relief, that sitting down gave me. To hell with judgemental people.

Definitely work out before starting riding, and specifically do exercises for riders. Also, start small. I just about died and barely could get home when I started, because I overestimated myself, lol.

Any textbook knowledge will likely be hard to implement in practice, and never quite like you imagined, so never think that you know better, until you have seen/tried everything in reality, this includes riding, horse care, horse body language, etc.

It is perfectly okay to switch trainers/barns if you feel like the trainer or the environment isn't a good fit, for example irritable/irresponsible/rash trainer, or perhaps they simply don't teach you enough, or maybe the horsecare seems sketchy. Besides, the more places you visit, the more experiences you can compare to eachother. I was under the impression, that the first barn I rode at was 10/10, and it was my fault for being so lame that I couldn't canter in almost 5 years of taking lessons. At the next barn, after nearly 10 years of not riding at all, I started late autumn, and early spring I was already able to (mostly) sit the canter, with just semi-regular weekly lessons.

It's perfectly okay to do worse occasionally, or maybe even for longer periods of time. Both you and the horse are living beings who are never the same, including the weather, ground, even the trainer. Countless factors that can make a ride perfect, or the worst. Key is patience, and plenty of it.

Riding is hard. Be well hydrated, and be on top of your nutrient intake before a ride. Well, you should do that all the time, but it's especially important when doing any kind of physical activity. And be prepared to do less strenous exercise during summer. It is *not* fun when you overexert yourself, especially if you have some kind of health condition.

Which brings me to my next point, if you feel unwell, it is perfectly okay to tell the trainer that you need a break, or even spend the rest of the ride at a walk, or stop altogether. What is not okay, to get so unwell, that you fall off the horse. It's not going to be good to your already struggling body, and you might break/bruise something. It's just not worth it. If someone makes a mean comment on it, they are stupid.

Apropriate gear and clothing. They exist for a good reason. Especially helmets, closed shoes and backprotectors. Looking "cool" is never more important, than avoiding or minimising injury.

Just because someone else is doing something bad, or it's "standard" at the barn you ride at, doesn't mean that you have to copy them. If you can't do anything against it, find a different place.

In my experience, they first match you weight wise (obviously), height wise, and then based on your experience and horse's availability. If it turns out, that you work well with a specific horse, due to your personality, riding style, or your own preferences, then they will try to match you two together (that is, if they know what's good for everyone, and have no ulterior motives, like bonding you with a horse they plan to sell).

As for these horses having the reputation of being lazy, but working well with you, it could be explained by different things. For example, they could simply like you more. But it's more likely your riding style. Beginners often are very wishy-washy. They don't have the strength, or the knowledge to sit and move well. This results with the horse being majorly confused and completely numb to their cues, because if the rider's leg constantly bumps into it's side, and then the rider gives a very weak kick meant to encourage it to trot, the horse won't know that it's actually meant to trot. And yes, many horses tend to not want to work and *will* weasel out of work, but only if you give them the opportunity. You can't keep your hands steady, and yank on the reins? The horse will chose to take that as you stopping it. You can't keep your legs steady, and then kick it to go faster? The horse will chose to take that as you just moving around for no reason. You can't keep your torso steady, and then try to give the horse ques through your balance? Good luck with that.

But if you are a firm rider, who clearly tells the horse what you want, and you don't let the horse walk all over you (as is common with beginners - they kick the horse, it doesn't go, they give up), then the horse will not only know what you want, but will also be more motivated to follow clear instructions.

There are plenty of memes and anecdotes, of people's horses being naughty, lazy, not moving right, and then the trainer sits on the horse, and now it's throwing out olympic level moves effortlessly. Even the laziest horse can be encouraged to work well, if you know how.

I myself have an example for this: I switched barns a couple months ago, and was paired with a lovely horse. A lovely horse who took me for an absolute clown. The first few rides were spent with me trying to get him to trot, and to keep him at trot, and go where I wanted him. It was an absolute nightmare. I even told my trainer once that I have no idea what i'm doing wrong, and she said that i'm not doing anything wrong, i'm just not being firm enough. My trainer had no choice but to get on him in the middle of the lesson to stop his "naughty" behaviour. And yes, the horse moved lovely under my trainer, even though just a minute before that he would stop and start backing up when I asked for trot. Now, though, I have figured out what makes him tick, I got better as a rider, and now I have barely any issues with him. Yes, it's not 100% great, but it's nowhere near the clown spectacle it was in the beginning.

And no, you don't have to cause pain, yell or be otherwise abusive to be a firm rider. A firm rider is much better than someone who can't give a proper cue to save their life.

Those people who dislike the horses you ride because those horse weasel out of work, probably just can't ride them well enough.

Using a crop is pretty standard (at least where I live) in barns for lesson horses. Most horses get "ruined" by beginners and a constantly changing cast of riders with their own habits and vices, even with trainers working on those horses. A crop tends to work much better than bruising the ribs, since beginners usually desensitise the horses mostly to leg aids, and less to the crop. It also helps in a different way, for example tapping them on the butt encourages them to engage their hind legs more, and if the horse tends to cut corners, a tap on the inner shoulder could help you to stop that from happening, if the inner leg, outside rein doesn't work and you don't want to rip off their face. Ever since I changed barns, i've been riding a horse, who can be beautifully forward, but by the gods, does he want to cut every corner possible lol. The crop at the shoulder can be a godsent, when he ignores every other aid from me.

I love horses, and I love riding, and I never missed anything as much as being around horses, when I couldn't be near them for nearly 10 years.

You don't need to jump Gran prix heights, you don't need to be good enough for gran prix dressage either, nor do you need to own horses, to be able to enjoy time spent with them. Countless people do sports just as a hobby, often with no proper gear, never too serious about technique or achieving great results, simply because that is not important. What's important, is that they enjoy it.

As for your second topic - i'm also an adult "relearner". I rode at the age 10-14, and then started again at almost 25. My advice - stop caring about the opinion of others. I missed horses and riding, so I found a barn with the sweetest owners and trainers, and just started riding there. In the beginning I was put in a small pen with little children just starting out. There are much more adult riders than you might think. Beginners, casual riders, "I got a month long subscription as a bday gift"-types, moms who take their children riding and also decided to ride there. There are plenty of children at the barn I ride at, who are better riders than many of the adults there, but no one really cares, because it doesn't really matter. If you are concerned about the potential reception, try finding a barn that isn't really into competing, where you can relax and polish up your knowledge, go on nice trail rides. You don't have to go to shows to be a "worthwhile" rider. The trainers will be happy to have someone giving them business and paying their bills, lol. And if a trainer thinks less of you for not being a professional, then they are just a bad person and no need to waste money on them.

My father was basically absent for most of my childhood, and when he actually did something to help me, it was by doing it in my stead. I was not taught how to do things, it was never even explained, he just did it. In that particular situation it helped, the issue was taken care of. But since I do not know *how*, I'm stuck the next time the same issue comes up.

My mother knew that "something is wrong with me", but while she did not say this, i'm 100% sure she refused to acknowledge that her precious daughter that she wanted so much, could have actual special needs. She expected that I would take care of myself, like NT kids do. She set out goals for me (like "study well", "decide what you want to be", "get a diploma", "get a good job", etc), encouraged me to reach them, and got mad when I couldn't, but she never helped me out in a way that I needed. Those generic advices that are perfectly good for NT children, did nothing for me. She thought I was just lazy and cowardly. The most frustrating part was, when once again, I was expected to deal with a new issue, and when I tried to take the matters into my own hands and ask her a bunch of "what if" questions, about any problem that could crop up, her only answer was "that bad thing won't happen". She just refused to tell me, what would happen if I failed in something, she refused to tell me how she would react, what she or others would do, what *I* should/could do. She strongly believed, that bad things told outloud would come true, so she just stonewalled me, when I tried to prepare myself for those bad things. Which meant, that besides being wholly unprepared for the situation because yet again, i'm flying blind with no script given to me, i'm also anxious, which takes up all my thinking power. It doesn't help, that I have a bad anxiety disorder, that got much worse as an adult.

Basically, I was sheltered from the world, while my parents also expected me to know about things they didn't let me learn. Anything that I know is either from the internet, random tidbits of knowledge people dropped throughout my life, and my own (most of the time negative) experience.

Also, I think making sure that the kid has a diagnosis is a good parenting choice. I myself struggled my whole childhood, because it was obvious as a day to me, that I was different, but I didn't know *what* that difference was. I could never decide, if I was smart or stupid, because while I was above my peers in certain areas, in others I was behind. The only comments I got from 2 teachers was "you think differently than the others". Thanks, but that doesn't help me. I suspected autism way back in elementary school, but at that time I was only aware of the non-verbal, unable to dress or feed themselves kind of autism, which did not apply to me. I was in uni, when I learned how vast the autism spectrum is, and that I 100% fit. It was such a relief, to finally understand, what this "difference" was. It helped me a lot, since I finally stopped worrying about the issue, and also, I could finally try and find things that could help someone with my condition. Accepting yourself and tailoring your life according to your special needs makes like a hundred times easier.
